name: Trichophytic closure

lead: Trichophytic closure is a way of closing the strip-harvest donor wound in a hair transplant (and facelift incisions) so hair grows through the scar and hides it. The payoff is a cleaner-looking back and sides, especially with a short haircut.

The wound edges are trimmed or stepped so follicles survive at the margin, and hair then grows through the healing scar. Published comparisons are small and mostly retrospective, such as a 2018 cohort of 46 facelift patients comparing W-plasty and straight-line closure on hairline scars.

paras: It is done by the surgeon at the time the donor strip is taken during a hair transplant, as part of how the wound is sutured. Patients see how the scar settles as the wound heals and hair grows through it over the following months. Variants such as double or asymmetric suture patterns are described for donor wounds.
It is a surgical closure with the usual wound risks, and scars can still be visible in some cases. It applies to strip (FUT) harvesting scars, not to follicle-by-follicle extraction.

angle.text: Hair transplant patients and surgeons use trichophytic closure after strip harvesting so hair grows through the donor scar, making a short haircut look cleaner. The camouflage is seen in the healed scar itself, and the supporting comparisons are small studies.

lead: Trichophytic closure is a way of stitching the donor wound after strip (FUT) hair transplant harvesting, and the incision lines of some facelifts, so that hair can grow through the scar instead of leaving a bare line. For someone who wears their hair short, or who expects to lose hair at the sides and back, a donor scar that hair covers is the difference between a transplant that is undetectable and one that is visible.[1]

In a trichophytic closure the surgeon prepares the wound edges so that hair follicles at the margin are preserved and hair emerges through or across the healed line. Wikipedia describes it as the latest closure method for strip harvesting and says it produces much finer donor scars.[1] Surgeons have published variants, including a double trichophytic closure with a wavy two-layer closure and an asymmetric dermal-subdermal suture for wide donor wounds.[2][3]

Published evidence consists of small comparative series, retrospective cohorts and case reports, among them a 46-patient comparison of W-plasty and straight-line trichophytic closure on facelift hairline scars and a registered 10-patient split-wound comparison at the donor site.[4][5]

paras: Strip harvesting removes a narrow band of hair-bearing skin from the back of the scalp, which is then dissected under magnification into follicular unit grafts, and the resulting defect is closed in a line.[1][6] Wikipedia describes the usual strip as roughly 1 to 1.5 cm wide and 15 to 30 cm long, with a thin linear scar that hair normally conceals, and notes that recovery takes about two weeks.[1] Follicular unit extraction (FUE) avoids the linear scar and leaves small punctate scars instead.[1]

Trichophytic closure is the name for closures designed to let hair grow through that line. Wikipedia calls it the latest closure method and says it yields much finer donor scars,[1] and Grokipedia describes the typical result as a fine linear scar of about 1 to 2 mm in width. Surgeons have also discussed whether the terms trichophytic and pre-trichophytic closure describe different techniques, a point raised in a letter in a plastic surgery journal.[6]

Hair transplantation as a modern field traces to the late 1950s, when New York dermatologist Norman Orentreich showed that grafts taken from the back of the scalp keep growing as they would in their original location, a principle known as donor dominance.[1] Strip harvesting later became the most common way to collect donor follicles, and the way its linear wound is closed has been a recurring subject of technique papers ever since.[1][7]

sections.h: How the closure differs from a standard linear closure
paras: In a conventional straight closure the wound edges meet at the skin surface and follicles at the margin may be cut or sit beneath the scar, so the healed line can appear as a hairless stripe. Trichophytic closure is described in the literature as an approach in which the edges are positioned so that follicles at the margin are retained and hair grows through or beside the healed line.[1][2] Variants differ in how the edge is trimmed or stepped and in how many suture layers carry the tension, which is the reason the double-layer wavy closure and the asymmetric dermal-subdermal suture were published as separate refinements for wide donor wounds.[2][3]

The related question of how a scar looks after healing depends on tension across the wound, scalp laxity and the width of the strip, topics that the donor-area literature addresses alongside the closure itself.[8][7]

A 2012 paper described a double trichophytic closure with a wavy two-layered closure, aimed at producing an optimal hair transplantation scar.[2] A 2013 letter in the same specialty journal described an asymmetric dermal-subdermal suture for trichophytic closure of wide donor wounds, where tension on a broad defect is the main concern.[3] A study of the donor area after follicular unit transplantation in India examined how donor scars look and presented techniques intended to make them cosmetically acceptable.[8]

In rhytidectomy, incisions run along the hairline behind and above the ear, and the scar there is visible if it widens or shifts the hairline. Surgeons have compared a straight-line trichophytic closure with a W-plasty version of the closure on occipital hairline scars.[4]

Trichophytic closure has been reported for scalp scars from cicatricial alopecia in a case report.[5] A separate case report described closing a 10 x 5 cm full-thickness scalp burn, caused by hair-coloring chemicals, with a skin-stretching method and trichophytic closure, followed by hair follicle transplantation to refine the remaining scars.[9]

Follicular unit extraction (FUE) removes individual units with small punches and leaves dot-like scars rather than a line, with recovery typically under a week and no suture removal. Wikipedia lists longer operating time, higher cost and a steep learning curve among its drawbacks, and notes that some surgeons report a lower proportion of successfully transplanted follicles than with strip harvesting.[1] People choosing between the two methods therefore weigh how visible a linear scar could be against these trade-offs, and trichophytic closure is one of the factors cited in favour of strip harvesting for people who want a fine donor line.[1]

The facelift cohort was carried out at the Buckingham Center for Facial Plastic Surgery in Austin, Texas, on 46 of 147 eligible patients operated on between June 2014 and August 2015. Twenty-three had a straight-line trichophytic closure and 23 had a W-plasty closure, all after the same extended high-SMAS facelift by one surgeon, with scars photographed at least a year later and scored by three blinded reviewers on a modified Manchester Scar Scale (0 best, 24 worst). Mean scores did not differ significantly between groups for any reviewer (for example 5.69 versus 5.86 for the first reviewer). No major complications were recorded and no patient complained about the occipital scar. The authors concluded that neither technique was superior and that a well-placed trichophytic incision closed without tension might be sufficient on its own. They listed limitations including the non-randomised design, subjective scoring and a mostly female, all-White population.[4]

A retrospective cohort at a facial plastic surgery center reviewed 46 rhytidectomy patients and compared W-plasty with traditional straight-line trichophytic closure on the posterior occipital hairline scar, evaluating aesthetic outcomes.[4] A split-wound study registered in 2012 (NCT01655602, n=10, listed as phase 1 with unknown status) compared trichophytic closure techniques on the two halves of the same hair transplant donor wound in patients with androgenetic alopecia.[10]

The remaining literature consists of technique descriptions, letters and case reports, such as the double closure, the asymmetric suture and the cicatricial alopecia report.[2][3][5] Sample sizes in these reports are small, and the studies differ in how scars were assessed.

timeline.event: Norman Orentreich begins free-graft experiments in male pattern baldness, establishing donor dominance.[1]
Strip excision begins to replace the older plug technique, and the stereo-microscope is introduced to dissect a single strip into micrografts.[1]
